About this citation

Published under the pseudonym Anti-Climacus. Kierkegaard's pseudonyms are not disguises but positions, and the authorship is part of the argument — so 'Kierkegaard says' flattens a distinction he constructed deliberately.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to The Sickness unto Death and files it under Existentialism.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Søren Kierkegaard

Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was a Danish religious author and critic of Christendom who wrote under pseudonyms exploring aesthetic, ethical, and religious existence. Inheriting a melancholy family fortune, he attacked Hegelian system and lukewarm official faith in Copenhagen.

Interpretation

Kierkegaard defines despair by what the self is doing rather than by how it feels. The self is a relation it must hold, and despair is the refusal to hold it in the form it has — wanting to be someone else, or not wanting to be a self at all. The "sickness unto death" is that the failure is in the part of a person that is supposed to be able to relate to everything else. Its severity is independent of how it presents.

Why it matters

The definition is uncomfortable because it identifies refusal rather than suffering. A person may be functioning well and still declining the self they have.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Despair is the sickness unto death — the…”?

“Despair is the sickness unto death — the…” comes from The Sickness unto Death (1849), attributed to Søren Kierkegaard.

What does Søren Kierkegaard mean by self?

To ask about the self is to ask what persists through experience, what can be known from the first-person point of view, and how character is formed. Some traditions treat the self as a substantial soul; others as a stream of experience, a social role, or a practical center of agency. This passage enters that discussion through self.
